---
id: cpp-leaderboard
title: Competition Leaderboard with STL Algorithms
difficulty: Medium
order: 1
tags: sort, nth_element, partition, unique, accumulate, lower_bound
time_limit: 2
---
## Statement
A robotics competition records `n` runs, each a line `TEAM SCORE TIME_MS`. A team's **best run** is its highest score, with ties broken by the lowest time. Compute, using STL algorithms rather than hand-written loops wherever you can:

1. `teams K`: the number of distinct teams.
2. The top 3 teams by best run (score descending, then time ascending, then name ascending), as `RANK. TEAM SCORE TIME`.
3. `median_best M`: the median of the best scores (for an even count, the lower median: element `(K-1)/2` in ascending order). Use `std::nth_element`.
4. `qualified Q`: the number of teams whose best score is ≥ the median. Use `std::partition` or `std::count_if`.
5. `total_runs_score S`: the sum of all scores, in a 64-bit accumulator.
6. For each query score `x` on the final line: the number of teams with best score **strictly greater** than `x`, using binary search on a sorted array of best scores.

Input: `n`, then n runs, then a line with `q` followed by q query scores. n is up to 300 000.

## Starter
```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <string>
#include <algorithm>
#include <numeric>

struct Run { std::string team; long long score; int time; };

int main() {
    std::ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    std::cin.tie(nullptr);
    int n;
    std::cin >> n;
    std::vector<Run> runs(n);
    for (auto& r : runs) std::cin >> r.team >> r.score >> r.time;
}
```

## Hints
- Sort the runs by `(team asc, score desc, time asc)` with `std::tie`. Then the first run of each team is its best one. `std::unique` with a "same team" predicate keeps exactly those.
- `std::partial_sort` with the ranking comparator gives just the top 3 in O(n log 3).
- Copy the best scores into a `std::vector<long long>` for `nth_element`, then sort a copy for the binary searches. "Strictly greater than x" is `end - upper_bound(x)`.
- `std::accumulate(..., 0LL, [](long long s, const Run& r) { return s + r.score; })`. The `0LL` matters!

## Solution
```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <string>
#include <algorithm>
#include <numeric>
#include <tuple>

struct Run { std::string team; long long score; int time; };

int main() {
    std::ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    std::cin.tie(nullptr);
    int n;
    std::cin >> n;
    std::vector<Run> runs(n);
    for (auto& r : runs) std::cin >> r.team >> r.score >> r.time;

    long long total = std::accumulate(runs.begin(), runs.end(), 0LL,
                                      [](long long s, const Run& r) { return s + r.score; });

    // best run per team: sort by team, then best first, and keep the first of each team
    std::sort(runs.begin(), runs.end(), [](const Run& a, const Run& b) {
        return std::tie(a.team, b.score, a.time) < std::tie(b.team, a.score, b.time);   // score desc via swapped args
    });
    runs.erase(std::unique(runs.begin(), runs.end(),
                           [](const Run& a, const Run& b) { return a.team == b.team; }),
               runs.end());
    std::size_t k = runs.size();
    std::cout << "teams " << k << '\n';

    auto rank_less = [](const Run& a, const Run& b) {
        return std::tie(b.score, a.time, a.team) < std::tie(a.score, b.time, b.team);
    };
    std::size_t top = std::min<std::size_t>(3, k);
    std::partial_sort(runs.begin(), runs.begin() + static_cast<long>(top), runs.end(), rank_less);
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < top; ++i)
        std::cout << i + 1 << ". " << runs[i].team << ' ' << runs[i].score << ' ' << runs[i].time << '\n';

    std::vector<long long> best(k);
    std::transform(runs.begin(), runs.end(), best.begin(), [](const Run& r) { return r.score; });
    auto mid = best.begin() + static_cast<long>((k - 1) / 2);
    std::nth_element(best.begin(), mid, best.end());
    long long median = *mid;
    std::cout << "median_best " << median << '\n';
    std::cout << "qualified " << std::count_if(best.begin(), best.end(), [&](long long s) { return s >= median; }) << '\n';
    std::cout << "total_runs_score " << total << '\n';

    std::sort(best.begin(), best.end());
    int q;
    std::cin >> q;
    for (int i = 0; i < q; ++i) {
        long long x;
        std::cin >> x;
        std::cout << (i ? " " : "") << (best.end() - std::upper_bound(best.begin(), best.end(), x));
    }
    std::cout << '\n';
}
```

Every step is a named algorithm with known complexity:
- `sort` + `unique` with a custom predicate does group-by-key "keep the best". The trick `std::tie(a.team, b.score, a.time) < std::tie(b.team, a.score, b.time)` swaps the operands of the middle key to sort it descending.
- `partial_sort` for the top 3 is O(n log 3).
- `nth_element` gives the median in O(n) average.
- `upper_bound` on the sorted best scores answers each query in O(log K).
- `accumulate` with a `0LL` initial value avoids the classic `int` overflow, since the sum of 300 000 scores of up to 10⁹ needs 64 bits.
